newsitem.title: UK: THIN GULF SALES LEAVE IRAQ SHORT OF EXPORT TARGET.
newsitem.headline: THIN GULF SALES LEAVE IRAQ SHORT OF EXPORT TARGET.

text.p: Paltry initial crude loadings from Iraq's Mina al Bakr terminal suggest Baghdad could struggle to reach its ambitious 30 million barrel end-August export target, traders said on Tuesday.

While a comprehensive liftings list for the Turkish port of Ceyhan has appeared, totalling 17.5 million barrels of Kirkuk crude, only two vessels are so far fixed to load in August from the Gulf al Bakr terminal.

The 340,000 tonne Jahre Ventura has been chartered by U.S. firm Bayoil to lift Basrah Light barrels on August 19 and the 325,000 tonne Stena Companion was fixed by U.S. firm Coastal for August 20, shipping brokers said.

A third very large crude carrier (VLCC) has been fixed by Coastal for September 6, after the deadline by which Iraq hopes to earn $1 billion from export sales under its "oil-for-food" deal with the United Nations.

Coastal's first vessel plus the Bayoil shipment should together load nearly five million barrels, leaving Iraq still some seven million, or three to four VLCCs, short of its 30 million barrel end-August target.
To meet its target by September 5 Iraq has to more than double the 670,000 barrels per day (bpd) it exported in the first six month term of the U.N. accord.
With 875,000 bpd planned for Ceyhan, and possibly more to come, traders estimate Iraq must load some 600,000 bpd from Mina al Bakr.

With Japanese buyers ruled out by Iraq for political reasons and Chinese firms discounting reports they might lift large quantities, there was little immediate sign the shortfall will be made up, brokers said.
"There have not been a lot of enquiries for shipping from Mina," said one, "and I don't think any vessels are being fixed quietly as we are not seeing VLCCs disappearing from the market."
"I haven't heard of any ships coming through the Strait of Hormuz at the moment," said a shipping source in the Gulf.
Russian oil companies have still to clarify exactly what they'll be lifting in August, if anything, from the Iraqi Gulf port in August.
"Its still unclear what we'll get. Its not yet stabilised," said one Russian trader.

The oil-for-food deal started last December and was renewed for another six months on June 8. It allows Iraq to sell $2.14 billion worth of oil, including pipeline fees, over six months in exchange for food and medicine.

Sales must be divided into two equal 90-day periods. After a two-month delay waiting for a revised aid distribution plan, Baghdad now has just 24 days to hit its $1 billion earnings target by September 5.
